items.title: Algeria severs diplomatic ties with UAE over ‘provocative, hostile’ actions
items.description: Algeria said on Thursday it had decided to sever diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates (UAE) after what it described as a series of “provocative or hostile” actions by Abu Dhabi despite “repeated warnings”. The Algerian foreign ministry said the UAE’s actions had reached a point where they could no longer be considered acceptable or tolerable and that it had “exhausted all means of preserving bilateral relations.” The UAE ambassador was summoned to the ministry, informed of the decision and given 48 hours to comply, the foreign ministry said. The UAE Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to an emailed request for comment. Relations between the two countries have come under growing strain in recent years, with Algerian media outlets sharply criticising the UAE and accusing it of seeking to sow regional discord. Algiers and Abu Dhabi have also taken differing positions on several regional issues. Algeria opposes normalisation with Israel , while the UAE and Algeria’s regional rival Morocco established diplomatic ties with Israel under the US-brokered Abraham Accords in 2020. The two countries are also on opposing sides of the decades-old Western Sahara dispute. The UAE supports Morocco’s claim to sovereignty over the territory where it has a consulate, while Algeria backs the Polisario Front, which seeks an independent Western Sahara. The two countries’ interests have increasingly intersected in the Sahel , where the UAE has expanded ties with several governments in recent years, while Algeria’s relations with some of its southern neighbours have become strained following a series of military coups. Algerian President Abdelmadjid said last year his country’s relations with all Gulf states were warm except for one — a thinly veiled reference to the UAE. He described ties with Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Oman and Qatar as “brotherly”, while accusing the unnamed country of meddling in Algeria’s internal affairs and seeking to destabilise it. In February, Algeria began the process of cancelling an air services agreement with the UAE that was signed in Abu Dhabi in May 2013.

items.title: Jackie Collins Wrote Her Own Revolution
items.description: Photographs by Dina Litovsky Once, when I was 15 years old and as awkward and skinny-legged as a baby giraffe, I was idling in a department store in central London when I saw the novelist Jackie Collins standing at the register. Can you imagine the aura emanating from her, like Hermès-scented magnetic waves? She was wearing animal print and a tailored jacket and had the kind of steely composure I’ve never managed to pull off in adulthood without straining something. Faced with one of my true idols, all I could do was gawk. I learned about sex when I was 8, but it wasn’t until several years later, when my best friend yanked me upstairs to show me a particularly juicy paragraph from her mother’s neon-pink copy of Hollywood Kids , that I learned about pleasure. Jackie—with apologies, I will call her Jackie throughout, because “Collins” feels just too formal for a woman who impressed upon me the existence of the clitoris— once told The New York Times that she published her first novel “in 1968, when no one was writing about sex but Philip Roth.” Which wasn’t strictly true, but at a moment when second-wave feminism and sexual liberation were uneasy bedfellows, Jackie simply wrote her own revolution. The World Is Full of Married Men , her debut, was a caustic social satire in which a wronged wife emerges triumphant; The Stud , out the following year, was a flashy potboiler about a trophy wife and nightclub owner with a rapacious sexual appetite who treats men like toys and exalts in her social and financial clout. Dina Litovsky for The Atlantic Jackie wrote 32 books in total, sold more than half a billion copies, and gained an indelible reputation as an airport novelist, the kind of writer whose books are equally devoured and disdained. But oh, what they did for me! In retrospect, I gained a slightly deluded understanding of what adulthood actually entailed. Jackie was a devoted Mickey Spillane fan, and her books tend to be stuffed with gangsters, serial killers, pornographers, and even freelance journalists who get paid in advance. But as an anatomist of Hollywood gender dynamics, no writer was sharper or more aspirational. Jackie’s heroines, as she wrote in an introduction to The World Is Full of Divorced Women (1975), “demand equality—sexual and otherwise.” She wrote about creative, ferocious women striving for power and getting it. Lucky Santangelo, a recurring character and a kind of alter ego, starts out as the neglected daughter of a crime boss and works her way up to become the head of a movie studio in 1990’s Lady Boss . Her characters carry on being fascinating and sexually active well past the age when other writers would have them tucked in bed with a crocheted blanket and a crossword puzzle. “In Jackie’s world, women’s real lives begin after forty,” the writer Helen Ellis observed of Hollywood Wives , the book that Jackie published at the age of 45, and that established her as a celebrity in her own right. Even if you hate women (many people do), hate explicit sex scenes, hate the kind of pulpy storytelling that has you still reading in a cold bath at midnight, you cannot help but admit that Jackie captured the entertainment industry like no one else. She seemed equally drawn to the business of movie production—the seedy dealmaking and kickbacks—as well as the rampant abuses of power embedded in the Hollywood system, both of which she exposed without hesitation. Writing in the heady 1980s, when movies were becoming brasher, dumber, and unrepentantly commercial, she scrutinized a creative industry at a notable low point, less in thrall to art than to profit. Although her novels made her a star, Jackie never considered herself fully part of Hollywood. Like a Reagan-era Margaret Mead, she took an anthropological approach. “I don’t live the Hollywood lifestyle,” she told Vanity Fair in 1995 . “I move in it. I’m an observer.” At parties, she would stalk the room listening for interesting tidbits, taking copious mental notes that she’d jot down later. Describing an A-list event in Hollywood Wives , Jackie drops in fragments of what one character calls “Hollywood conversation,” dialogue that evokes a world where money and desire meld: “ ‘He pays me, I think it turns him on,’ said the redhead in the mink-trimmed cape.” So accurate was her portrayal that when Hollywood Wives was published, Jackie noted, “The ladies of Hollywood had their drivers and housekeepers lining up at the bookstores to get an early copy,” both furious that their gilded sanctum had been breached and desperate to pinpoint which character was based on which real person. Hollywood , as a geographical term at least, is misleading: Jackie’s characters mostly work and play in Beverly Hills, a city of 30,000 or so extremely wealthy residents enclosed by Los Angeles. Formerly a lima-bean farm, then a failed oil field, Beverly Hills was developed into lots for housing around the same time that the movie industry headed west, in the early 20th century. When the silent-film stars Mary Pickford and Douglas Fairbanks moved into a spectacular former hunting lodge on Summit Drive in 1920—the press immediately named it “Pickfair”—they helped establish Beverly Hills as a nexus of celebrity glamour and industry cachet. Jackie genuinely loved the neighborhood for its clean white lines and endless sky, but she was also drawn to everything it contained beneath the surface: its roiling currents of fame, power, and degradation. Early this summer, I traveled from London, where Jackie was born, to the enclave where she made her name. As a child of the ’80s, I was nostalgic for the maximalist era of shoulder pads, Giorgio perfume, and animal print. (Jackie loved big cats for their beauty and power, was convinced she’d been a panther in a previous life, and decorated her house and herself in leopard spots.) But as a cultural critic, I also wanted to revisit the era of moviemaking that Jackie had described in her novels. The ’80s saw a wave of corporate consolidation; venerable studios were gobbled up by behemoths from other industries. (Columbia Pictures was briefly a division of Coca-Cola.) This led to sillier, more crowd-pleasing movies. Even so, Hollywood was at the apex of its power, the global influence of filmmaking more potent than ever. Today, the center of cultural power and attention is shifting away from Los Angeles. Traditional storytelling has lost ground to what the consulting firm McKinsey calls “user-generated content”—TikTok and YouTube videos in which people talk enthusiastically about peptides and skinny-maxxing and the cruel feminization of the male life force. Dina Litovsky for The Atlantic The Gucci storefront on Rodeo Drive. The protagonists of Jackie’s Hollywood novels frequently visit the street’s luxury boutiques to arm themselves for the soft warfare of self-presentation. As a teenager, I had learned from Jackie’s books to expect that adulthood for women would be a series of hard-won triumphs that lead toward power. (She also suggested that midlife would involve a lot of stalking around restaurants while wearing crepe Halston jumpsuits and enough gold jewelry to sink a yacht, but I have long since made peace with neutral basics.) I am 43, roughly the age when Jackie’s heroines enter their prime, and when she herself did. I am very tired, having spent the past 14 months working, raising two 5-year-olds, promoting a book, and falling into existential mires of despair over the degenerating state of world affairs. A small, quiet part of my brain wondered whether tracing Jackie’s literary footsteps might reinvigorate my sense of what’s possible. Or at least demonstrate that her dreams for women—that they can have creative fulfillment, families, and happiness, as she did—might be somewhat more realistic now than they were 40 years ago. H ollywood Wives was published in 1983, a good two decades before reality television turned exposing the lives of the wealthy, married, and highly maintained into a Bravo gold mine. We’re accustomed to such excess now, but back then, Jackie’s gossipy revelations—$50 panties, discreet plastic surgeons in Palm Springs, society grandes dames who used to be French call girls—seemed otherworldly. The primary antiheroine in the book is the delightfully unlikable Elaine Conti (imagine a hornier, more desperate Becky Sharp), the 39-year-old wife of a movie star, Ross, whose last film bombed at the box office. There’s also a former gigolo on the brink of movie stardom, a buxom man-eater who wants to be taken seriously as an actress, and a serial killer who calls himself the “Keeper of the Order.” But for me at least, the book stands out for its portrayal of early-’80s Beverly Hills as a high-society Thunderdome, where everyone is scratching and clawing for status. In addition to the titular wives, who are drawn with both humanity and mild disdain, Jackie offers up a number of female characters operating in what she describes as the “Big Boys’ Club” of the movie industry: Sadie LaSalle, one of the most powerful and fearsome agents in town, and Montana Gray, a writer trying to save her screenplay from the clutches of a ruthless producer. This is a world where power-lunching demands tactical precision. Elaine’s mission throughout the book is to restore Ross’s A-list status, with buzzy parties the couple can’t afford and a standing Friday lunch reservation at Ma Maison, where “anybody who was anybody and in town invariably showed up.” Ma Maison closed in 1985, and so the first place I went to test out the current state of power-dining was the Polo Lounge, a clubby salon situated toward the back of the spectacularly retro Beverly Hills Hotel. In Hollywood Husbands , Jackie’s 1986 follow-up, the handsome and promiscuous talk-show host Jack Python regularly meets his best friends for breakfast there, where they occupy Table One, “a cosy leather booth directly facing the entrance.” Table placement, Jackie emphasizes, is everything—“The back of this restaurant is Siberia,” one model tells another late in the book. “Land of the underachievers. Don’t even glance in that direction.” I was not placed at Table One. I was seated just outside what seemed to be the main dining room, next to an elderly couple and a 12-year-old wearing a World Cup hoodie having pancakes by himself. Through the doorway, I could see men in button-downs and golf shirts conversing chummily; I started to feel slightly psychotic glimmers of envy and shame at being shut out from whatever they were brokering. The server’s eyes expressed gentle but unmistakable pity. A handsome Englishman was seated at a nearby table but immediately sensed defeat and asked to be moved to the terrace, where the sun shines regardless of a diner’s Variety profile, stock portfolio, or follower count. Dina Litovsky for The Atlantic Dina Litovsky for The Atlantic Failure is galvanizing, I tried to remember from Jackie’s books, as long as you don’t let it break you. For much of her early life, Jackie wasn’t known for her writing or her feline fixation. (A plaque engraved with a panther marks her place in the celebrity crypt at Westwood Village Memorial Park Cemetery, where she was interred after her death, in 2015; the image is accompanied by the words SHE GAVE A GREAT DEAL OF PEOPLE A GREAT DEAL OF PLEASURE. ) She came of age as the taller, ungainly younger sister of Joan, an almond-eyed, preternaturally composed actress who made her Hollywood debut starring alongside Bette Davis in 1955’s The Virgin Queen . Joan and Jackie had grown up together in a basement apartment in dingy postwar London, the daughters of a dance teacher and a talent agent whose parties, Jackie once said, were where she first became aware of how men talk about women when they think no one’s listening. “I get an awful inferiority complex when I’m with Joan,” the teenage Jackie wrote in her diary. In a photo of the pair together from 1955 , Joan stands front and center, insouciant in a fur coat, while Jackie looks at the camera semi-apologetically from behind her. Jackie was, however, entrepreneurial; by the age of 13, inspired by Harold Robbins and Henry Miller, she had a sideline writing sex scenes longhand and charging her classmates to read them. When Joan’s career took her to Hollywood, Jackie followed, moving with her sister to an apartment in the Chateau Marmont hotel, and having a brief fling—at 15—with the 29-year-old Marlon Brando. (He was “only my height, and kind of fat,” she noted in her journal, and also recorded that he called her “sincere, sweet, and luscious.”) But Jackie couldn’t get a work permit and so reluctantly returned to England, where she appeared in a handful of schlocky B movies before marrying the businessman Wallace Austin at 22. Four years later, Austin’s drug addiction had led the couple to divorce, and he died of an overdose shortly after. Dina Litovsky for The Atlantic People pose for photographs in front of the Paul Smith Pink Wall on Melrose Avenue, a landmark for the Instagram era. It was Jackie’s second husband, the producer and nightclub owner Oscar Lerman, who encouraged her to pursue writing, and to draw inspiration from the vivid social scenes the couple mixed in. (At one of her husband’s clubs, she told The Hollywood Reporter , Lerman had to put a guard outside the men’s room because teenage girls kept following movie stars in to offer them sexual favors.) At 31, she published The World Is Full of Married Men , which was an immediate best seller in the United Kingdom and promptly banned in Australia for its inventive array of four-letter words; the next year, the romance novelist Barbara Cartland lambasted her new novel , The Stud , as “awful, terrible, it’s evil really.” Jackie and Lerman relocated to Los Angeles in 1980, and if you walk down the Beverly Hills Hotel’s unabashedly red-carpeted stairs and under a gloriously cinematic green-and-white striped awning, then stroll to the bottom of the hill, and wander for about 10 minutes beneath towering palm trees, you will arrive at the house that Jackie’s “awful, terrible” books built. Only a modest-seeming driveway was visible from the street. The place is now available for rent (for the trivial sum of $175,000 a month), and when I say that I begged the real-estate agent to let me view it, please know that I really and truly groveled. I spent months emailing a man who assured me that he was entreating the owners (real-estate developers who’d bought it after her death, gutted it, remodeled all the interiors) on my behalf—but to no avail. So instead I examined the signs affixed to palm trees warning me that I was on camera, to ensure the security of the neighborhood’s current residents, who—unlike the movie stars and moguls of Jackie’s day—are apparently financiers, minor Middle Eastern royals, and crypto magnates. (The current owner of the Pickfair mansion, I later learned, is the technology corporation Unicom Global, which uses it for conferences and events.) But based on the listing, archival photographs, and the author photo on Jackie’s many hardcovers, I can tell you that it’s a 22,000-square-foot museum of a mansion, a defiant middle finger to the critics who belittled her for writing “bonkbusters,” and a visual testament to her success. The interiors are now predominantly beige, but in Jackie’s day, the pillows were all animal print. She designed the house around a huge rectangular swimming pool after seeing David Hockney’s A Bigger Splash in London. On her book jackets, she stands, radiant and shoulder-padded, next to the cool blue water and her imposing white box of a home. But she also took great pride in being a hands-on mother, cooking at home for her three daughters, doing school drop-offs in her silver Mustang, and keeping her children away from the sleazy Hollywood scenes she chronicled. Dina Litovsky for The Atlantic In Jackie’s novels, characters mostly work and play in Beverly Hills, a nexus of celebrity glamour and movie-industry cachet since the 1920s. Right as Jackie’s writing started appearing on the best-seller list, Joan’s acting career was floundering—in 1977, she appeared in the dismal sci-fi horror Empire of the Ants , playing a land developer set on by giant irradiated insects. It was Jackie who revived her sister’s reputation, after Joan was cast as the lead in the movie adaptation of The Stud . (A hit in Britain, the movie paved the way for Joan to get her most indelible American role, as Alexis Colby in Dynasty .) The charged sense of competition between the pair continued apace; in a 1988 Vanity Fair profile of both sisters , Dominick Dunne noted that a publicist had instructed him to dedicate equal copy to each woman, while also citing the rumors that Silver Anderson, the prickly 47-year-old TV star in Hollywood Husbands , was based on Joan. Mindful of the security cameras, I walked quickly past Jackie’s house to a restaurant in downtown Beverly Hills called Bacari, where I took out my notebook and tried my hand at Jackie-style anthropology. At the table next to me, a talent agent was trying to lure another agent away from a major conglomerate, where she was unhappy. “They keep trying to buy us off with ice-cream socials,” she said to him plaintively. “Everyone is on a diet!” The conversation turned to her stable of clients, who all seemed to be social-media stars. She spoke proudly about one woman she represented who, under her mentorship, went from having 700,000 followers to more than 1 million. “That’s the kind of nurturing I bring to my job,” she said. The man asked her if she might be able to double her client list in the first three months; to help her in the effort, he could offer her a “digital assistant—no person.” He paid the bill. “Let’s get those wheels turning,” he said, ushering her out, and I wondered what Jackie would make of this version of Hollywood, with its brand-activation opportunities and AI-drafted emails, where celebrity is its own art form and product is paramount. In Jackie’s Hollywood novels, Rodeo Drive—my next stop—is where the women of Beverly Hills go to arm themselves for the soft warfare of self-presentation. When every outfit, every hairdo, is minutely studied for signs of decline, keeping up appearances is essential. In Hollywood Husbands , Poppy Solomon, the secretary turned fourth wife of a studio head, gets ready for parties in much the same way General Patton commanded the Third Army: with ostentatious and pleasurable aggression. (“She wore a turquoise frilled, strapless dress, and many real diamonds. Her new tits protruded nicely.”) The day I was there, the picture-perfect palms gently fluttering down Rodeo bore signs for an upcoming car show, which seemed unnecessary given that every day brings a parade of tricked-out vehicles: I watched a procession of Porsches, G-Wagons, two separate Maybachs with hydraulic suspension systems that had them bouncing up and down like sugared-up toddlers. No one was actually shopping, despite the lavish window displays. Instead, everyone was posing for pictures, wearing outfits they’d put together for this exact purpose and drafting husbands and friends to play photographer. A slender blond woman clutching a tan Birkin pouted while reclining against a lamppost outside Stefano Ricci. Someone whispered that she was a Russian influencer with a superstar-athlete partner, which seemed perfectly plausible, but outside the subset of her followers, how would the rest of us know? Dina Litovsky for The Atlantic A scene outside the Chateau Marmont in West Hollywood, the hotel Jackie moved into with her sister, Joan, in her teens Dina Litovsky for The Atlantic Jackie lived in the Beverly Hills Hotel when she moved back to Los Angeles in 1980. I was accompanied by a photographer, Dina, who approached the influencer to take her picture, but the woman scuttled away like a cartoon mouse. Something odd was happening, we quickly realized: Everyone was out posing in public, but no one wanted to cede control of how they might be perceived. When Dina tried to take photos of the Beverly Hills Hotel from a public sidewalk, a voice instantly came over a loudspeaker warning her to stop. In a weak attempt to consider some of the box-office excess of 1980s Hollywood ( Footloose , Top Gun , Beverly Hills Cop ), I booked us a Paramount Pictures studio tour, but when I asked a publicist about Dina bringing her camera, I was told approval would be required, a studio representative would accompany us, and anything said on the tour could not be quoted. (All that’s worth saying about what followed is that while being driven around the lot where Citizen Kane , Breakfast at Tiffany’s , and Chinatown were shot, the most enthralling thing we saw was the plasticky interior set from the CBS reboot of Matlock .) Jackie would find Hollywood’s new power dynamics perplexing: Many of her female characters are writers and reporters on the movie-celebrity beat, who see their job as pushing past the sanitized narratives that publicists try to present. But as media jobs have dwindled, influencers have stepped in to fill a void. Why would you trust a possibly unfriendly reporter with access to an actor or a director or a TV set when you can invite a photogenic social-media star to a premiere and be assured that they’ll rave about whatever they see to their hundreds of thousands of followers? In Hollywood Husbands , Silver, the soap star possibly based on Joan, is interviewed by an English journalist, “a middle-aged woman with brittle looks and dyed yellow hair” who sucks up to her subjects as energetically in person as she tears them apart in print. “So what?” Silver thinks. “Someone had once said As long as they spell your name right .” The internet has long since retooled this bargain. And what are celebrities now, anyway? During my four days in Beverly Hills, which Jackie portrays as a superstar playground—Clint Eastwood, Jack Lemmon, Richard Gere, and Tom Selleck all feature in one lunch scene at Ma Maison—I saw not a single recognizably famous person. A dozen or so women looked similar enough to Kim Kardashian to stop me short; they were clearly modeled after her, but the image fell apart on second glance. One night I went to dinner at Funke, a purported newish hot spot for stars (Gwyneth Paltrow is a fan) where the chef used to have his own show on the disastrous short-form streaming platform Quibi. No sightings. My L.A.-based friends advised heading east, to Los Feliz and Silver Lake, or west, to Venice and Santa Monica. Beverly Hills today is a bastion of the über-wealthy—Jeff Bezos owns the estate built by Jack Warner of Warner Bros.—and a drop-by for people who come to pose for Instagram. Like SoHo in New York and Notting Hill in London, the place feels like a simulacrum of a film set, where everyone is perpetually performing for unseen audiences and nothing feels quite real. Dina Litovsky for The Atlantic Hollywood, at the apex of its cultural power when Jackie was writing, is a very different touring experience now. In her books, Jackie is unsentimental about creative work. Her characters tend to hustle for money and power, not self-indulgent awards or critical acclaim. When good movies get made, it’s largely by accident, because someone took their eye off the ball. But one character in Hollywood Wives seems to genuinely care about the integrity of the work she makes: Montana Gray, the tall, raven-haired, strikingly offbeat writer who—coincidentally—has a biography that seems a lot like Jackie’s own. By 15, Montana is a worldly soul who’s traveled the globe, learned French and Italian, and had two affairs. After spending a few years in bohemian circles, she meets the much older film director Neil Gray in Paris and falls in love with him. She helps him get sober and working again; he encourages her to write. At the start of the novel, her gritty screenplay, Street People , is the talk of Hollywood, with actors and agents fighting for copies. And, because Montana is the wife of a major director, no one can accept that she actually wrote it. “Good-looking women had roles in life and they were supposed to stick to them,” Jackie writes. “They could be movie stars, models, housewives, hookers, but God forbid they should skirt onto what was strictly regarded as Big Boys’ Territory. Writing a major movie for a major director was Big Boys’ Territory. And in their own petty little way everyone wanted to let her know that.” When Neil pushes to cast the craggy movie star George Lancaster in a leading role in the film, Montana acquiesces reluctantly—he can’t act—only for George to assume that she’s a secretary the very first time they meet. “I’m Montana Gray,” she tells him. “I wrote Street People .” “You did?” he replies. “My, my, things sure are changing around here. I could still use that coffee, little lady.” You might wonder whether things are actually different for women in Hollywood today. The statistics are still dismal : 8.1 percent of the 100 highest-grossing movies in 2025 were directed by women, a seven-year low, and the percentage of movies with any major female characters at all fell from 39 percent the previous year to 36 percent. But TV is faring better: More than a third of all streaming shows now have at least one female creator. One of those women is Lisa Joy, formerly a writer and co-creator of HBO’s adaptation of Westworld , a futuristic sci-fi show with a notably feminist question at its core: What might men do to women if those women didn’t seem fully human and the men thought they could get away with it? In 2019, Joy and her husband, the screenwriter and producer Jonathan Nolan, signed a reported $150 million deal to create shows for Amazon, including the acclaimed video-game adaptation Fallout and an upcoming TV version of Rebecca Yarros’s blockbuster romantasy series, Fourth Wing . Jackie would have liked the all-caps plaque on Joy’s desk— I’M CEO, BITCH —that greeted me in the Hollywood offices of her production company, a glass-walled room facing the Capitol Records building. Like Montana, Joy is impossibly glamorous and all too familiar with having people presume that her accomplishments are secretly a man’s. So much of Westworld , she told me, came from her experiences being the lone woman in what felt like male playgrounds. But, like Jackie, she’s convinced that writing a different world gets us one step closer to manifesting it. Dina Litovsky for The Atlantic The screenwriter and director Lisa Joy at the offices of Kilter Films, the production company she runs with her husband, Jonathan Nolan Post-MeToo, Joy said, she’s noticed some really positive changes, such as a junior writer she knows speaking out against a serial harasser whom no one had ever dared confront before, and who was subsequently fired. But reminders abound of all the ways in which things have stayed the same. “There are so many yacht trips I’ve heard about for male directors and writers,” she said. “I don’t know why they all get yachts, but there doesn’t ever seem to be a woman invited. But fuck the yachts, you know? They make you seasick. They’re no fun. Let’s make the reality we want.” I left Joy’s office feeling energized by her work, by her enthusiasm, by her determination. And then, as I was crossing Hollywood Boulevard, the universe gave me a palpable reality check: a 50-foot billboard advertising Louis C.K.’s upcoming comedy special for Netflix. On my last morning in L.A., I went downstairs to get breakfast in my hotel, and ended up sitting near two men who were discussing potential merchandising deals for one of their clients. “Makeup is really splintered; it’s a challenging category for sure,” one said. “But fragrance is booming. What about hair?” The client has a personal connection to hair, the other said excitedly. ( Who among us? I thought.) The first man proceeded to expound on how hair brands are working quickly to address the issues—thinning, shedding—that can come from GLP‑1 use. The other circled back to his client, whom he talked about with such reverence that I leaned closer, convinced she was a huge household name. “Her pull on her community is so strong,” he said. “What feeds her passion is serving her community and improving people’s lives. She’s built for this.” Only by the end of the conversation, and after much furtive Googling on my part, did it become clear whom they were talking about: a Goth-makeup influencer on TikTok who has more than 6 million followers. You could argue that the content-creator model has democratized entertainment and broken down conventional gatekeeping, enabling anyone with a ring light, a front-facing camera, and a compelling personality to find their following. I don’t disagree. But it’s also restored youth and overconfidence as the preeminent characteristics for women on camera. Whereas what I’ve always loved about Jackie’s books is how they enshrine success and power as being hard-won and worth the hustle—and the wait. Midlife is when things get interesting for her characters, because they know the stakes they’re playing for, and they’ve accrued enough wisdom and battle scars to rival and even occasionally best the Big Boys. But the waning public interest in traditional storytelling (because you’re reading this, I’ll diplomatically ignore the even gloomier fate of the written word) has other consequences too. If you’re someone who doesn’t just love movies and TV shows but has felt genuinely changed by some of them, it’s hard not to mourn what we lose when our mass culture has all the bells and whistles of entertainment—hair, makeup, stars, product placement—but none of the curiosity about human predicaments underpinning it. Jackie’s work was berated during her lifetime by critics (“It starts off as nothing and ends as nothing” — Clive James) and high-school English teachers like mine (“trash”), but it graphically exposed a Hollywood full of sexual harassment and gender inequity. Not least, it imagined alternative paths for women to pursue. Now her books are mostly out of fashion; when I stopped by the Barnes & Noble inside the Grove, where Jackie liked to shop before going to the movies, the store had not a single copy of any of her novels. I was feeling despondent when I went for a last outing, to Mariposa: one of Jackie’s favorite restaurants, where she met for lunch each week with her closest friends, an elegant dining room tucked into the basement of the Neiman Marcus Beverly Hills. I had learned in emailing beforehand that Jackie was still a much-loved figure there. I was met by the store’s manager of brand experience, Mary Kate Steinmiller, who looks exactly like the actress Malin Akerman and used to be a fashion editor at Teen Vogue . She took me downstairs to Jackie’s favorite blue booth. Dina Litovsky for The Atlantic A couple dressed in designer outfits dine at the Mariposa, a restaurant tucked into the basement of the Neiman Marcus in Beverly Hills, where Jackie met with her closest friends weekly for lunch. For days, I’d been traipsing through Beverly Hills trying to find a little spiritual proximity to Jackie, and here it was, on the lower floor, by the beauty counters. Groups of women wearing Christian Dior tennis whites and Pucci wrap dresses chatted ebulliently over cocktails (it was 12:15 p.m.). Every table featured floral arrangements nicer than the ones at my wedding. Over in a corner, an older couple wearing acid-green designer outfits sat absorbed in each other. A table of women told me that Mariposa was their country club. They had known and liked Jackie, but quickly pushed back against the lingering stereotype of the Hollywood Wife. One was a high-powered divorce attorney. Another was a sports photographer. The restaurant was gorgeous (and don’t sleep on the lobster salad), but it was also clear what it meant to these women: community, affirmation, a clubby dining room of their own. Watching them, I felt as though what Jackie’s novels had promised might actually be true: If you can muster enough ambition and persistence to keep pushing through, the payoff could well be worth the wait. Travel Notes Spago Ma Maison, immortalized in Hollywood Wives , is long gone, but in 1982 its star chef, a telegenic Austrian named Wolfgang Puck, left to open Spago on the Sunset Strip, redefining L.A. dining in the process. The original location closed decades ago, but Spago Beverly Hills lives on, with its twinkly lit courtyard, casual-luxe menu (Jackie loved the smoked-salmon pizza and wrote it into multiple books), and luxe-luxe prices. If you never get to go to the Academy Awards’ Governors Ball, which Puck has catered for more than three decades, this is at least a chance to eat stardust by association. 176 N. Canon Drive, Beverly Hills CA, 90210 Bob’s Coffee and Doughnuts Doughnuts and Hollywood physiques go together like deep-dish and Ozempic. Don’t let that keep you away from Bob’s, a 56-year-old stand inside the historic Los Angeles Farmers Market, where writers have come to eat and procrastinate since the 1930s. According to legend, Robert Altman used to have breakfast here, scribbling away under the slatted awnings. And the doughnuts really are great—pillowy and sugar-sprinkled. Fun fact: A branded Farmers Market tote bag costs $2, compared with $50 for one at the nearby Erewhon. 6333 W. 3rd St., Stall #450, Los Angeles CA, 90036 Hollywood Books Is this tiny spot on Melrose a bookstore in the conventional sense? Not really, at least not if you’re looking for a popular novel or Belle Burden’s monster-hit memoir, Strangers . At Hollywood Books, the shelves are stacked with secondhand art volumes and reissued classics. Despite—because of?—its unfussed approach to business, the store has become extremely chic among the literary girlies of Los Angeles; at one point it hosted an event for the supermodel Kaia Gerber’s book club, Library Science. I left with a copy of Picture , Lillian Ross’s 1952 analysis of the clash between art and corporate interests in moviemaking, just to remember that things were ever thus. 6917 Melrose Ave., Los Angeles CA 90038 Wrapstar I can’t endorse the wraps or salads here, because I had only a sparkling water. But for eavesdropping like Jackie, you can’t beat the location—across the street from William Morris Endeavor’s boxy Beverly Hills headquarters, and next door to Cipriani. Sit, snoop, rubberneck. (Yes, wraps are passé, but power agents sometimes need sad-desk lunches that you can eat with one hand while scrolling through social media, just like the rest of us.) 356 N. Camden Dr., Beverly Hills CA, 90210 Bar Funke Funke regrettably did not provide any celebrity sightings, but it did furnish a gorgeous twist on a margarita, made with Sicilian-blood-orange bitters and prickly pear. The rooftop, after you enter through a jasmine-strewn trellis, looks out over the palms and offices of Beverly Hills, but from my spot at the bar, all I wanted to stare at were the pink quartzite counters and Chef Evan Funke’s elaborate collection of Amaro aperitifs. Jackie’s literary alter ego, the glamorous and hot-blooded Italian businesswoman Lucky Santangelo, would have appreciated both. 9388 S. Santa Monica Blvd., Beverly Hills CA 90210 Mariposa Here’s to the ladies who lunch, and to playing one in this delightful department-store-basement restaurant, with its velvety blue booths and popovers accompanied by strawberry butter. The waitstaff are lovely, the diners’ outfits are extraordinary, and the food—lobster salad, crab cakes, tuna tartare—is opulent and calorie-conscious, and so good you’ll be wondering why the guests aren’t eating more of it. If I ever die and get to (at least) purgatory, I hope it’s a little like Mariposa. 9700 Wilshire Blvd., Beverly Hills CA, 90210 This article appears in the October 2026 print edition with the headline “Jackie Oh!” When you buy a book using a link on this page, we receive a commission. Thank you for supporting The Atlantic.

items.title: Région du Nakambé : L’ADCT présente ses investissements de 8,5 milliards FCFA en faveur du bien-être des populations
items.description: L’Agence nationale d’appui au développement des collectivités territoriales (ADCT) a transformé le quotidien des populations des communes de la région du Nakambé. En effet, l’ADCT a misé sur des infrastructures utiles et durables au profit des populations grâce à un investissement de 8,5 milliards de FCFA. Santé, état civil, hydraulique, éducation, les infrastructures visitées les 8 et 9 septembre 2026 témoignent d’un accompagnement qui contribue à améliorer les conditions de vie des populations. De Koupéla à Boussouma, en passant par Gomtenga, dans la région du Nakambé, les réalisations de l’Agence nationale d’appui au développement des collectivités territoriales (ADCT) se donnent à voir sur le terrain. Les bureaux de l'état civil Le soleil est déjà haut dans le ciel lorsque la délégation de l’ADCT et les journalistes arrivent au secteur 5 de Koupéla. Ici, un bâtiment se distingue au milieu des habitations : le Centre de santé et de promotion sociale (CSPS). L’ouvrage a été réalisé en 2024, mais ce n’est qu’en février 2026 qu’il a effectivement ouvert ses portes. Depuis, les consultations se succèdent et les populations des environs n’ont plus besoin de parcourir de longues distances pour accéder aux soins. Dans les locaux du CSPS, Jacques Kaboré, infirmier-chef, revient sur le changement apporté par l’ouverture de la structure. « Auparavant, les populations devaient parcourir de longues distances pour accéder aux services de santé. Désormais, elles sont beaucoup plus proches du centre, ce qui réduit à la fois les distances et les coûts de déplacement », a-t-il confié. Le médecin-chef Jacques Kaboré félicitant l'ADCT pour ses réalisations Pour les femmes enceintes, les enfants et les autres patients, la proximité du centre constitue un véritable avantage. Le suivi des grossesses est facilité et les enfants peuvent notamment bénéficier des services de vaccination. Mais derrière cette satisfaction, quelques besoins demeurent. « Le personnel est encore insuffisant et le CSPS a besoin de matériel médico-technique supplémentaire. Nous avons des difficultés d’approvisionnement en médicaments au niveau du dépôt », a indiqué M. Kaboré. Le PDS de Koupela appréciant les réalisations de l'ADCT Moumouni Sagnon, président de la délégation spéciale de la commune de Koupéla, a pour sa part signifié que la commune ne disposait auparavant que d’un seul CSPS. « Avec l’augmentation de la population et de la fréquentation, il devenait difficile pour cette seule structure de répondre à l’ensemble des besoins. Il était donc nécessaire de réaliser un deuxième CSPS », a-t-il souligné. Dans le cadre du premier tirage de 2022, 45 millions de francs CFA ont été mobilisés pour la réalisation du dispensaire, des latrines et du forage. Un mur de clôture est actuellement en construction dans le cadre du Programme pour la Résilience, la Gouvernance Locale et les Services de Base (PREGOLS) 2026. Sur ce site du secteur 5 de Koupéla, le montant global des infrastructures réalisées dépasse 76 millions de francs CFA. Pour assurer leur entretien, un comité de gestion, le COGES, a été mis en place. Salle d'attente au CSPS de Koupela Le président de la délégation spéciale, Moumouni Sagnon, s’est par ailleurs réjoui de l’accompagnement de l’ADCT qui, selon lui, ne se limite pas au domaine sanitaire. « Nous considérons l’ADCT comme un partenaire sûr. Depuis le début de notre collaboration, nous entretenons de bonnes relations et la collaboration se déroule dans de bonnes conditions », se réjouit-il. À Gomtenga, une maternité qui change les habitudes La route se poursuit ensuite vers Gomtenga, dans la commune de Dialgaye. Ici aussi, une infrastructure sanitaire attire l’attention. Une maternité réalisée avec l’accompagnement de l’ADCT. Lilougou Naaba mesurant le changement apporté par cette nouvelle infrastructure Avant son implantation, les femmes de Gomtenga et des environs devaient se rendre à Dialgaye pour certains soins. Le Lilougou Naaba mesure le changement apporté par cette nouvelle infrastructure. « Avant, il n’y avait pas de maternité, tous partaient à Dialgaye pour les soins. C’est éloigné et la route n’est pas bonne », a-t-il expliqué. La nouvelle maternité rapproche donc les services de santé des populations et devrait faciliter particulièrement la prise en charge des femmes. Pour autant, le besoin ne s’arrête pas à la construction du bâtiment. Le Lilougou Naaba souhaite désormais que la structure soit dotée d’équipements médicaux pour lui permettre de fonctionner dans de meilleures conditions. « Nous remercions l’ADCT pour son accompagnement multiforme en faveur de Dialgaye », a-t-il indiqué. À Boussouma, l’état civil retrouve de meilleures conditions de travail Dernière étape de cette tournée dans la région du Nakambé, Boussouma, située à environ 35 kilomètres de Tenkodogo. La commune compte 16 villages administratifs et bénéficie également de l’appui de l’ADCT. Salle de l'état civil À la mairie, un nouveau bâtiment destiné aux services de l’état civil est occupé depuis le début du mois de janvier 2026. À l’intérieur, cinq bureaux accueillent différents services. Les agents disposent désormais de matériel informatique, de mobilier de bureau et des équipements nécessaires à l’accomplissement de leurs missions. En moyenne, une vingtaine d’actes sont délivrés chaque jour. Goudouma Jacques Kima, secrétaire général de la commune, se souvient encore des conditions de travail dans l’ancien bâtiment. « Avant la construction de ce bâtiment, les services de l’état civil étaient installés dans un bâtiment qui datait d’une vingtaine d’années et qui ne répondait plus véritablement aux conditions de travail », a-t-il raconté. Lorsque les pluies s’abattaient sur la commune, la situation devenait particulièrement préoccupante. Les agents devaient déplacer les documents afin de les protéger contre les eaux. Aujourd’hui, le nouveau bâtiment apporte un véritable soulagement à l’administration communale. Le secrétaire général exprime sa reconnaissance à l’ADCT pour son accompagnement. 8,5 milliards FCFA mobilisés dans le Nakambé Depuis l’opérationnalisation de l’agence régionale en 2011, 8,5 milliards de francs CFA ont été mobilisés au profit des communes de la région du Nakambé, selon Joseph Kaboré, directeur de l’agence régionale de l’ADCT dans le Nakambé. Un forage construit au secteur 5 de Koupela Les financements portent principalement sur les infrastructures scolaires, sanitaires et les forages communautaires. À cela s’ajoutent des bâtiments administratifs et des boutiques de rue, qui contribuent notamment au renforcement des ressources fiscales des communes. Les projets ne sont pas choisis au hasard. Ils correspondent aux besoins exprimés par les populations et portés par les communes auprès de l’ADCT. Au terme des deux jours de visite, le directeur régional de l’ADCT Nakambé, Joseph Kaboré, se dit satisfait de constater que les infrastructures réalisées sont effectivement utilisées. « Quand nous voyons que ce sont des infrastructures qui sont très utilisées, cela fait que nous sommes très heureux d’avoir été utiles pour la population », a-t-il affirmé. Forte mobilisation des habitants de Gomtenga Mais pour que ces investissements continuent de servir les générations futures, l’entretien reste un enjeu majeur. Joseph Kaboré appelle ainsi les communes et les bénéficiaires à accorder davantage d’importance à la maintenance des ouvrages. « L’ADCT travaille d’ailleurs à la mise en place de Gestion, Entretien et Maintenance (GEM), un outil destiné à faciliter la gestion et la préservation des infrastructures au niveau des collectivités », a-t-il laissé entendre. De Koupéla à Gomtenga, puis à Boussouma, les bâtiments visités racontent l'histoire d’infrastructures pensées pour répondre à des besoins locaux. Pour l’ADCT, l’objectif est de poursuivre cette dynamique et renforcer l’accompagnement des collectivités afin de contribuer davantage au développement local. Lire aussi : Région du Gulmu : L’ADCT investit 15 milliards FCFA pour l’école et la santé Sidziguin Irène Corinne SAWADOGO Minute.bf

items.title: PRA-UEMOA-Guinée : Boubacar Yacine Diallo, une reconnaissance régionale d’un parcours au service de la presse guinéenne
items.description: Par Abdoulaye Bouka BARRY- C’est une nouvelle consécration pour Boubacar Yacine Diallo et, au-delà de sa personne, une reconnaissance de l’expertise guinéenne en matière de régulation des médias. Élu, les 31 août et 1er septembre 2026 à Conakry, président de la Plateforme des Régulateurs de l’Audiovisuel des pays membres de l’UEMOA, élargie à la Guinée (PRA-UEMOA-Guinée), le président de la Haute Autorité de la Communication entame un mandat de deux ans à la tête de cette instance régionale. Une élection que les superviseurs de la HAC dans la zone spéciale de Conakry considèrent comme l’aboutissement d’un parcours consacré aux médias, au journalisme et à la régulation. Ce mardi 8 septembre 2026, dans les locaux de la Haute Autorité de la Communication à Conakry, l’ambiance avait des allures de retrouvailles entre professionnels du même secteur. Mais la rencontre revêtait une dimension particulière. Treize journalistes superviseurs de la HAC, mobilisés dans les treize communes de la capitale à l’occasion des élections législatives et communales du 31 mai 2026, sont venus présenter leurs félicitations à Boubacar Yacine Diallo, désormais président en exercice de la PRA-UEMOA-Guinée. À travers cette démarche, ces professionnels de terrain ont voulu saluer une élection qui, selon eux, ne doit rien au hasard. Elle vient plutôt récompenser plusieurs années d’engagement au service de la communication, de la presse et de la régulation audiovisuelle. Une élection qui « ne constitue pas une surprise » Portée par la voix de leur porte-parole, Samory Keita, la délégation des treize superviseurs a d’abord tenu à rappeler le parcours du président de la HAC et la cohérence de son accession à cette nouvelle responsabilité. Dans son adresse, Samory Keita a notamment insisté sur le chemin parcouru par Boubacar Yacine Diallo, estimant que son élection à la tête de la plateforme régionale s’inscrit dans la continuité d’une carrière construite au contact des médias et de leurs réalités. « Au nom des treize (13) superviseurs de la HAC de Conakry, nous vous adressons nos sincères et chaleureuses félicitations à l’occasion de votre accession à la présidence de la Plateforme des Régulateurs de l’Audiovisuel des pays membres de l’UEMOA, élargie à la Guinée (PRA-UEMOA-Guinée). Votre accession à cette responsabilité ne constitue pas pour nous une surprise. Elle s’inscrit dans la continuité d’un parcours professionnel particulièrement riche, construit au fil des années au service de la communication, des médias et de la régulation. » Pour les superviseurs, cette nouvelle responsabilité régionale vient ainsi prolonger le travail entrepris par Boubacar Yacine Diallo à la tête de la HAC. Cette reconnaissance prend une dimension supplémentaire lorsqu’elle est replacée dans le contexte des dernières années, marquées par plusieurs échéances politiques et électorales majeures en Guinée. Du référendum aux élections législatives et communales : la HAC au cœur des rendez-vous électoraux Depuis son arrivée à la tête de la Haute Autorité de la Communication, Boubacar Yacine Diallo a été confronté à l’un des exercices les plus sensibles de la régulation des médias : accompagner les grands rendez-vous électoraux tout en veillant au respect des règles encadrant leur couverture médiatique. Référendum constitutionnel, élection présidentielle, élections communales et législatives : autant de scrutins au cours desquels la HAC a dû composer avec la multiplication des acteurs, la diversité des lignes éditoriales et la forte sensibilité du débat politique. Dans ce dispositif, les superviseurs déployés sur le terrain ont constitué un maillon essentiel de la chaîne de régulation. C’est précisément ce rôle et cette évolution institutionnelle que Samory Keita a voulu mettre en lumière, en rappelant que la Guinée avait vécu, à la fin du mois d’août, un moment particulier avec l’organisation à Conakry de la 12ᵉ Assemblée générale de la PRA-UEMOA-Guinée. L’élection de Boubacar Yacine Diallo est intervenue après deux années passées à la vice-présidence de cette plateforme. Pour les superviseurs, cette progression témoigne d’une confiance progressivement acquise au sein de l’espace régional. « Pour nous, superviseurs des 13 communes de Conakry, ce parcours témoigne de votre constance, votre engagement en faveur des médias, de leur professionnalisation et de la consolidation des mécanismes de régulation. Vous voir aujourd’hui à la tête de cette plateforme régionale est donc pour nous la reconnaissance d’un parcours et d’une expertise », a souligné Samory Keita. Une distinction qui dépasse le cadre de la HAC Au-delà de la satisfaction personnelle qu’elle peut représenter pour le président de la HAC, cette élection est également perçue par les superviseurs comme une opportunité pour la Guinée de renforcer sa présence dans les instances régionales de régulation. Dans leur message, ils ont ainsi donné à cette accession une portée nationale, estimant qu’elle contribue à renforcer la visibilité de l’expertise guinéenne dans le domaine de la régulation audiovisuelle. Samory Keita l’a exprimé sans détour, en soulignant que la nouvelle responsabilité confiée au président de la HAC constitue, à leurs yeux, « une fierté nationale ». « Elle offre à la Guinée une visibilité supplémentaire au sein de l’espace régional et témoigne de la confiance accordée à son organe national de régulation. Nous souhaitons que cette distinction ouvre la voie à davantage de rayonnement de notre institution sur le plan régional et international, et qu’elle constitue un précédent appelé à se perpétuer. » Face à ses superviseurs, Boubacar Yacine Diallo n’a pas caché sa satisfaction. Le président de la HAC a d’abord salué une démarche qu’il considère comme un signe fort de reconnaissance du travail accompli au sein de l’institution. Avec une certaine émotion, il a également relevé que cette délégation de treize superviseurs était la première organisation structurée à venir lui présenter officiellement ses félicitations après son élection à la tête de la plateforme régionale. Le président de la HAC y voit surtout le résultat d’un effort collectif, loin de toute réussite individuelle. « Je voudrais me réjouir de cette rencontre. Je suis particulièrement heureux de recevoir vos félicitations à l’occasion de l’élection de la Haute Autorité de la Communication à la fonction de président en exercice de la PRA-UEMOA-Guinée. Ce résultat, on pourrait le dire comme ça, est la consécration du travail que mes collègues commissaires et moi-même avons fait pendant plusieurs années ici à la Haute Autorité de la Communication. Vous êtes les premiers, comme groupe organisé, à nous transmettre vos félicitations. Nous en sommes ravis. Au nom de mes collègues, je voudrais vous transmettre toute notre satisfaction. » Une réponse qui traduit une volonté de partager cette reconnaissance avec l’ensemble des commissaires de la HAC et, plus largement, avec les équipes qui ont accompagné l’institution dans ses différentes missions. La rencontre aura également été l’occasion pour Boubacar Yacine Diallo de retourner les félicitations à ceux qui, quelques mois plus tôt, étaient en première ligne lors des élections législatives et communales. Le président de la HAC a tenu à rendre hommage au travail réalisé par les treize superviseurs dans un contexte où la surveillance du traitement médiatique des élections exigeait à la fois rigueur, impartialité et capacité de dialogue. S’adressant directement à eux, il a souligné la difficulté de leur mission : superviser des médias privés aux lignes éditoriales différentes, tout en préservant leur liberté et en veillant au respect des exigences de la régulation. « Les commissaires me chargent de vous renouveler notre confiance. Pendant les élections passées, vous avez fait montre d’un professionnalisme exemplaire et d’une honnêteté irréprochable. Vous nous avez prouvé qu’il y a encore des journalistes dans ce pays qui peuvent assumer, au-delà de leur profession, des fonctions aussi contraignantes, aussi délicates, que superviser une élection au niveau des médias privés qui ont des lignes éditoriales diverses en fonction des objectifs de leur création », a-t-il déclaré. Dans la même logique, Boubacar Yacine Diallo a salué leur capacité à maintenir un équilibre entre les exigences des professionnels des médias et celles des acteurs politiques engagés dans les différentes compétitions électorales. « Vous avez su ménager à la fois les professionnels des médias qui sont jaloux de leur liberté et les hommes politiques qui se lancent à la conquête du pouvoir pour les élections législatives, pour être député, et pour les élections communales, pour être soit maire, soit conseiller communal. Je vous redis toute notre satisfaction, je vous redis toute notre confiance », a-t-il ajouté. L’élection de Boubacar Yacine Diallo à la tête de la PRA-UEMOA-Guinée intervient ainsi à un moment où les enjeux liés à la régulation audiovisuelle prennent une importance croissante dans l’espace ouest-africain. Pour celui qui a consacré une grande partie de sa carrière au journalisme et à la défense des intérêts de la profession, cette nouvelle fonction ouvre désormais un autre chapitre : celui d’une responsabilité régionale qui place la Guinée au cœur des réflexions sur l’avenir de la régulation des médias. Mais au-delà des titres et des fonctions, son parcours reste étroitement associé à l’histoire récente de la presse guinéenne. De journaliste à responsable du secteur des médias, puis président de la Haute Autorité de la Communication, Boubacar Yacine Diallo a traversé plusieurs générations et plusieurs transformations du paysage médiatique national. Son action à la tête de la HAC s’est notamment inscrite dans les moments les plus sensibles de la vie publique guinéenne, avec la nécessité permanente de trouver un point d’équilibre entre liberté de la presse, responsabilité éditoriale, pluralisme de l’information et respect du cadre légal. Son accession à la présidence de la PRA-UEMOA-Guinée apparaît dès lors comme bien plus qu’un changement de fonction. Elle constitue une reconnaissance régionale d’une trajectoire nationale et place désormais Boubacar Yacine Diallo devant un nouveau défi : faire entendre, au sein de l’espace communautaire, la voix d’une régulation guinéenne appelée à poursuivre sa mue et à renforcer son influence. Abdoulaye Bouka Barry L’article PRA-UEMOA-Guinée : Boubacar Yacine Diallo, une reconnaissance régionale d’un parcours au service de la presse guinéenne est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: El Supremo ve en la ‘ley de nietos’ un “peligro fundado, real y serio” de afectar a la “objetividad” de las elecciones
items.description: El Tribunal Supremo considera que la inscripción en el censo electoral de los nacionalizados por la Ley de Memoria Democrática, la llamada ley de nietos , genera “un peligro fundado, real y serio de poder afectar gravemente a la objetividad y transparencia del proceso electoral”. Y esa posibilidad causaría “un daño irreversible a la rectitud y corrección de aquel”, sostiene el Supremo, que teme que otorgar el derecho al voto a los nuevos nacionalizados afecte al “resultado electoral deseado por los españoles que ya figuran inscritos correctamente en el censo electoral”. Así lo expone la Sala de lo Contencioso-Administrativo en los autos que han dado lugar a la suspensión del derecho al voto de quienes han obtenido la nacionalidad por ser hijos o nietos de españoles que abandonaron el país entre el 18 de julio de 1936 y el 31 de diciembre de 1955. La magistrada Alicia Millán ha emitido un voto particular en el que discrepa de sus compañeros. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Bab al-Mandab — key oil route facing growing Houthi threat
items.description: Yemen’s Houthis have launched a major ground assault around the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the Red Sea chokepoint that has become vital for Saudi oil exports during the Middle East war. With hundreds dead in fighting, and the Houthis exchanging strikes and counter-strikes with Saudi Arabia, AFP examines the flashpoint waterway that is normally one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes. ‘Gate of Tears’ Known as the “Gate of Tears” in Arabic because of its history of shipwrecks, the strait sits at the southern tip of the Red Sea, connecting it with the Gulf of Aden in the Indian Ocean. About 100 kilometres long and just 30km wide at its narrowest point, it separates Yemen on the Arabian Peninsula from Djibouti and Eritrea on the Horn of Africa. Strategic trade route With the Red Sea linking maritime trade between Europe and Asia, the strait is usually one of the world’s busiest shipping lane s. Oil tankers and cargo ships use it to reach the Mediterranean via the Suez Canal, shortening journeys between Asia and Europe and North America by thousands of kilometres. In 2024, as the Houthis attacked Red Sea shipping during the Gaza war, Suez Canal traffic fell sharply and has yet to recover, according to IMF PortWatch data analysed by AFP . Total transits dropped from 26,895 vessels in 2023, or 73.7 per day, to 14,498 in 2024 and 14,070 in 2025. The Houthis, claiming to act in solidarity with the Palestinians, were attacking ships that they said had links to Israel. Average transits for January-August 2026 stood at 40.8 vessels per day, still little more than half the pre-crisis level. The Houthis do not control the coastal areas bordering Bab al-Mandab, but they hold the large port city of Hodeida further north. On Monday, a Yemeni military source told AFP they had seized the coastal city of Mokha. Since declaring a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia in July, the rebels have repeatedly attacked Saudi ships in the Red Sea. They have denied that they seek to follow Iran’s blockade of the Strait of Hormuz , the mouth of the energy-rich Gulf, by trying to close the Bab al-Mandab or impose transit fees. Analysis by the Institute for the Study of War said the Houthis are “attacking Saudi Arabia’s ability to export oil in order to try to raise Saudi political and economic costs to an untenable level”, forcing Riyadh to halt military operations. Oil exports at risk Even before the Middle East war, the Bab al-Mandab was a major route for oil shipments, with the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) saying 12 per cent of world oil shipments transited in 2023. Although Houthi attacks during the Gaza conflict cut ship numbers dramatically, Iran’s closure of Hormuz turned the Bab al-Mandab into a vital alternative route. A map showing the locations of the Bab al-Mandeb strait, Strait of Hormuz and Suez Canal. — made using ArcGIS Saudi crude shipments from the Red Sea port of Yanbu surged after the war began, averaging around 3.8 million barrels per day between March and July — about five times their pre-war level — commodities data firm Kpler estimated. On a daily basis, that was equivalent to about 4.5pc of the crude oil processed by refineries worldwide in 2025. But shipments fell sharply to 1.5m barrels per day in August, after the Houthis resumed attacks on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea in July. Preliminary Kpler data put exports at 2.44m barrels per day in the first nine days of September, although that figure remains subject to revision. Andreas Krieg, a security expert at King’s College London, said the “biggest danger is not necessarily physical closure of Bab al-Mandab but persistent uncertainty”. “I would expect prolonged instability to suppress traffic through Suez and impose significant costs on Egypt, while adding time and expense to Europe-Asia trade,” he added. Yemen’s conflict returns The Middle East war erupted on February 28 when the United States and Israel launched attacks on Iran, prompting Tehran to retaliate with strikes across the region. Then in July, the Houthis triggered a return to hostilities in Yemen when they let an Iranian plane land in defiance of Saudi control of Yemeni airspace. The government retaliated by striking the airport, with ensuing exchanges unravelling a 2022 truce in Yemen’s long-running civil war. Since then, the Houthis have declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia, attacking its tankers and its territory. Now, as the group edges closer to the Bab al-Mandab, Iran and its allied groups are increasing their capacity to choke Gulf oil exports. Kreig said Houthi gains over the Bab al-Mandab would give them “extraordinary strategic leverage”. “Controlling the coast would strengthen Houthi maritime coercion, but the ability to impose risk on shipping already exists without territorial control of the strait,” he added.

items.title: Bamako : Mieux organiser la circulation avant le prochain drame
items.description: © Internet Deux morts, plusieurs blessés, c’est le bilan d’un accident causé par un camion de livraison hors de contrôle au rond-point de l’ENSUP le 1 er septembre. L’accident rappelle une évidence que Bamako repousse depuis trop longtemps : tous les véhicules ne peuvent pas continuer à partager les mêmes voies, aux mêmes heures, avec les mêmes règles. Certes, les poids lourds sont indispensables à l’approvisionnement de la capitale et aux chantiers. Mais leur utilité n’efface pas les risques. En 2025, l’ANASER a recensé 7 691 accidents, 8 863 blessés et 648 morts au Mali. Des restrictions existent déjà à Bamako. Les horaires et itinéraires sont encadrés et, depuis mai, les camions-bennes sont interdits de circulation entre 20 heures et 6 heures. Le problème n’est donc plus seulement d’édicter des règles, mais de les rendre cohérentes, applicables et contrôlées. Il faut définir des plages adaptées, imposer des itinéraires réellement respectés, développer les gares périphériques et les voies de contournement, puis privilégier des véhicules plus légers pour certaines livraisons urbaines. D’ailleurs, l’ANASER prévoit d’ailleurs une étude sur les sections à risque pour les poids lourds à Bamako. Même exigence pour les camions de vidange. Voir une citerne mal étanche laisser couler des eaux usées dans la circulation ne devrait jamais devenir une scène ordinaire. Étanchéité, contrôle technique, sanctions et sites de dépotage accessibles doivent aller ensemble. Une capitale ne protège pas ses habitants en leur demandant seulement d’être prudents. Elle doit organiser les risques avant qu’un nouveau trajet banal ne se transforme encore en lieu de deuil.

'Is judiciary so weak that you wish to strengthen it?' IHC CJ asks as KP counsel justifies PTI’s Sept 27 march
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Chief Justice of the Islamabad High Court (IHC) Sardar Muhammad Sarfraz Dogar on Thursday admonished Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Advocate General Shah Faisal Utmankhel after he described PTI’s September 27 protest call as a move in support of the judiciary. The PTI has announced a nationwide protest on Sept 27 to demand the release of party founder Imran Khan and mobilise people for the supremacy of the Constitution. A citizen, Waqas Ahmed, had challenged the planned move in the IHC on the grounds that the protest could disrupt routine life, traffic and business activities in the federal capital. On Tuesday, CJ Dogar decided to form a larger bench to hear the petition, observing the sensitive nature of the matter. As Utmankhel appeared before the IHC on Thursday, he contended that the PTI long march was also being organised in support of the judiciary. “Thank you very much for wanting to strengthen the judiciary,” the chief justice remarked sarcastically, before asking: “Is the judiciary so weak that you wish to strengthen it?” CJ Dogar observed that the judiciary was not so weak as to require the support of a political party. At the outset of the hearing, Attorney General for Pakistan Mansoor Usman Awan contended that government machinery could not be used for political protests. AGP Awan said no government officer should comply with an order contrary to the Constitution and the law. However, he added that it would be difficult for an officer to refuse an order issued by the chief executive of a province, referring to KP Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, who belongs to the PTI. “If this court issues an order, it will be binding on anyone holding an executive position,” the attorney general said, adding that clear judicial directives would make it easier for civil servants to implement them. The chief justice asked whether the KP chief secretary and inspector general of police (IGP) were not bound by an IHC order issued in 2024. “Yes, absolutely; they are bound to implement that order,” AGP Awan replied. He said state resources could not be used for political activities, even if a protest was peaceful. Referring to PTI’s 2024 protest, he said the then-chief minister of KP had led the demonstration himself. The 2024 order had come days before a PTI power show planned for late November, barring the party from holding any protests or rallies. However, the party went ahead with the protest as scheduled, leading to a day of clashes between security forces and protesters in Islamabad’s Red Zone that ended with the PTI leadership’s hasty retreat. The bench then summoned the KP AG to the rostrum and asked him to explain the provincial government’s position. The KP AG said he had received the notice only a day earlier and was not even aware of the contents of the petition. He also objected to the petition’s maintainability, arguing that the matter was premature. CJ Dogar, however, asked him to respond after hearing AGP Awan’s submissions. The KP law officer maintained that orders of superior courts had not always been complied with in the past and objected to remarks concerning the province’s chief executive, who, he pointed out, was not a party to the case. He also questioned the premise of the petition, asking why the proposed long march was being perceived as an “attack”. In an apparent reference to previous IHC orders directing that meetings between Imran and his family and party leadership be arranged, the KP AG said the court had repeatedly issued such directions, but they had not been complied with. He added that “dozens” of contempt petitions had subsequently been filed. He requested two days to prepare his arguments. The chief justice declined the request and gave him until the following day, directing him to at least begin his arguments at the next hearing. When the chief justice referred to media coverage of the court’s previous order, the KP AG said that, given his responsibilities, he did not have time to watch television. At one point, the petitioner’s counsel objected to the KP AG’s appearance, asking whether he was representing a convicted prisoner. The court directed the KP AG to produce, at the next hearing, a record of action taken in the past against those who had violated court orders. The bench also summoned the inspector generals and chief secretaries of all four provinces, along with other relevant officials, for the next hearing and issued fresh notices to ensure their appearance. The court directed all the summoned officials to appear again on September 11 (Friday).

items.title: Guinée-Sierra Leone : Conakry et Freetown renforcent leur coopération autour des frontières, de l’immigration et de l’économie
items.description: Le Premier ministre, chef du gouvernement, Amadou Oury Bah, a reçu mercredi 9 septembre 2026, à la Primature, le vice-président de la République de Sierra Leone, Dr Mohamed Juldeh Jalloh, en visite de travail à Conakry. Une rencontre placée sous le signe de la solidarité, du renforcement de la coopération bilatérale et de la consolidation des relations de bon voisinage entre les deux pays. Au cœur des échanges figuraient notamment les suites du tragique éboulement survenu à la décharge de Dar-es-Salam, les questions migratoires, la sécurisation des frontières ainsi que le renforcement de la coopération économique et sécuritaire entre Conakry et Freetown. A l’issue de la rencontre, le Premier ministre guinéen a salué la démarche des autorités sierra-léonaises, tout en rappelant les liens historiques, géographiques et humains qui unissent les deux peuples. « C’est un honneur et un plaisir pour la Guinée de recevoir cette délégation d’un pays frère, d’un pays voisin », a déclaré Amadou Oury Bah, avant de souligner que la rencontre devait permettre de rechercher, dans un esprit fraternel, des réponses aux préoccupations communes. La question des populations affectées par le drame de Dar-es-Salam, mais aussi celle de l’immigration et de la sécurisation des frontières, ont occupé une place importante dans les discussions. Pour le chef du gouvernement, ces sujets concernent directement les populations vivant de part et d’autre de la frontière et nécessitent une approche concertée entre les deux États. Ces échanges s’inscrivent également dans le prolongement du sommet extraordinaire des chefs d’État de l’Union du fleuve Mano, tenu à Conakry le 16 mars dernier. Amadou Oury Bah estime que la visite du vice-président sierra-léonais pourrait contribuer à donner un nouvel élan à cette organisation régionale, notamment sur les plans institutionnel et organisationnel. De son côté, Dr Mohamed Juldeh Jalloh a expliqué que sa présence à Conakry répondait d’abord à une volonté du président Julius Maada Bio, du gouvernement et du peuple sierra-léonais de présenter leurs condoléances aux familles des victimes de l’éboulement de Dar-es-Salam, survenu dans la nuit du 22 au 23 août. Le vice-président sierra-léonais a également salué la réaction des autorités guinéennes dans la gestion des opérations de secours et la prise en charge des victimes, parmi lesquelles figuraient des ressortissants sierra-léonais. « Je voudrais remercier chaleureusement le gouvernement guinéen ainsi que Son Excellence le président de la République, le général Mamadi Doumbouya, pour la rapidité et l’efficacité des secours », a-t-il déclaré, estimant que cette réaction témoignait de la profondeur des liens de fraternité entre les deux pays. Au-delà de cet épisode douloureux, Freetown et Conakry ont convenu de poursuivre les efforts visant à apaiser les tensions frontalières et à renforcer leur coopération. La question migratoire a notamment fait l’objet d’échanges approfondis. Selon Mohamed Juldeh Jalloh, les deux gouvernements ont déjà travaillé sur des mesures qui devraient être annoncées prochainement. La coopération économique figure également parmi les priorités évoquées. Le vice-président sierra-léonais a annoncé de prochaines discussions entre les ministres du Commerce et de l’Industrie des deux pays, avec l’ambition d’organiser une foire ou un salon commercial commun. Une initiative qui, selon lui, devrait favoriser davantage les échanges économiques et contribuer au processus d’intégration sous-régionale. Cette visite intervient ainsi dans un contexte marqué par la volonté affichée de Conakry et de Freetown de renforcer leur politique de bon voisinage. A travers le dialogue sur les questions migratoires et frontalières, mais aussi par le développement des échanges économiques et sécuritaires, les deux pays entendent consolider une coopération fondée sur leur histoire commune, leur proximité géographique et leur communauté de destin.

items.title: Initiative présidentielle pour la Santé : Immersion patriotique pour 1 876 nouveaux agents de santé
items.description: Pendant que les centres médicaux communaux sont en finition et équipement, les agents de santé ex sont à l’école de la discipline militaire et du patriotisme. « 𝑁𝑜𝑢𝑠 𝑣𝑜𝑢𝑙𝑜𝑛𝑠 𝑑𝑢 𝑝𝑒𝑟𝑠𝑜𝑛𝑛𝑒𝑙 𝑠𝑜𝑖𝑔𝑛𝑎𝑛𝑡 𝑡𝑟è𝑠 𝑟é𝑠𝑖𝑙𝑖𝑒𝑛𝑡, 𝑝𝑎𝑡𝑟𝑖𝑜𝑡𝑖𝑞𝑢𝑒, 𝑠𝑜𝑢𝑐𝑖𝑒𝑢𝑥 𝑑𝑢 𝑚𝑎𝑙𝑎𝑑𝑒, 𝑠𝑜𝑢𝑐𝑖𝑒𝑢𝑥 𝑑𝑒 𝑙𝑎 𝑔𝑒𝑠𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛 𝑑𝑒𝑠 é𝑞𝑢𝑖𝑝𝑒𝑚𝑒𝑛𝑡𝑠 ». 944 personnels de santé, sur un total de 1 876 recrutés dans le cadre de l’Initiative Présidentielle pour la Santé (IPS), en immersion patriotique du 6 au 16 septembre 2026, à l’Institut national de formation des personnels de l’éducation (INFPE) de Loumbila. La rentrée s’est déroulée en présence du representant Bureau national des Grands Projets du Burkina (BN-GPB), des Coordonnateurs de l’IPS, ainsi que des Forces de Défense et de Sécurité et de représentants du ministère de la Santé. Recrues d’une session spéciale de 2025, ces agents sont notamment des médecins généralistes, des pharmaciens généralistes, des chirurgiens-dentistes généralistes, des médecins spécialistes, des pharmaciens spécialistes, des infirmiers, des sages-femmes, des technologistes biomédicaux, des techniciens d’hygiène hospitalière et des techniciens supérieurs en imagerie médicale. Ce recrutement spécial a été accordé au ministère de la Santé afin de permettre aux Centres médicaux communaux, actuellement en phase de finition, d’être opérationnels dès leur ouverture. « A l’issue de cette formation, nous voulons du personnel soignant très résilient, patriotique, soucieux du malade, soucieux du bien-être de sa communauté, de son cadre de travail, soucieux de la gestion des équipements, nous voulons que quand un malade se présente dans un centre médical, que depuis l’accueil, il puisse se sentir à l’aise », a indiqué le camarade coordonnateur national, Drissa TRAORE. Selon le camarade Capitaine Ariel RAMDE, Commandant du Bataillon de commandement et de soutien de la Garde républicaine, « l’immersion patriotique consistera à leur inculquer les valeurs de savoir-vivre et de savoir-être militaire. Ces valeurs vont leur servir dans leur quotidien, dans leur travail et partout où ils seront, parce qu’elles vont permettre de lever des barrières et de renforcer la cohésion ». Le camarade chef de cabinet du BN-GPB, Adama Loé TRAORÉ, représentant le Directeur exécutif, a souligné que le recrutement spécial ainsi que leur immersion, s’inscrivent dans la vision du chef de l’État, le Camarade capitaine Ibrahim TRAORÉ, qui souhaite renforcer le patriotisme chez les Burkinabè d’aujourd’hui en vue d’assurer un développement durable. En rappel, le Conseil des ministres a adopté, en octobre 2025, le plan « 1 000 x 5 », visant le recrutement de 5 000 agents de santé et paramédicaux en appui à l’Initiative présidentielle pour la Santé. « Nous pensons que c’est vraiment une bonne chose parce qu’ il faut une équipe unie et soudée… Nous estimons que c’est une opportunité pour le ministère de la santé à saisir pour faire participer tout le personnel nouvellement recruté »,a indiqué le camarade directeur des ressources humaines du ministère de la santé, Mamadou TRAORE. DCRP/BN-GPB

items.title: Trump Is Preparing for a Long War
items.description: To hear the Trump administration tell it, the war with Iran is all but over. U.S. military posture tells a different story: Naval forces are being positioned for a sustained presence at least through the end of the year, keeping open the option of escalation. The Navy is moving aircraft carriers, its signature asset, around the globe so that two can be deployed in and around the Persian Gulf in the final months of this year, giving the United States the ability to hit both Iran and Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, who have recently fired barrages of missiles at Saudi Arabia. Meanwhile, the Army has extended the deployment of elements of the 82nd Airborne Division, which are already in the region, because of “operational requirements.” The conflict, now in its seventh month, has already lasted far longer than the president’s initial predictions of victory within a few weeks. And senior officials have recently downplayed the scale of the conflict in the apparent hope that it will recede from the headlines. Vice President Vance claimed to reporters last week that the U.S. is not at war at all. Soon after, President Trump referred to the conflict as “small potatoes,” though he has since termed it a war. After Iran targeted a U.S. warship, the Navy sank five Iranian crude-oil tankers on Tuesday, according to U.S. Central Command. With no talks under way, and no end to the hostilities in sight, the Navy is staying on a war footing indefinitely, adding to the severe burden already placed on the Navy and on U.S. munitions stockpiles. The unusually long deployment of the carrier USS Abraham Lincoln, whose crew spent 264 consecutive days at sea and dropped more than 1.5 million pounds of ordnance, was plagued with food and supply shortages, plumbing problems, and declining morale. The Lincoln eventually departed for Thailand, relieved by USS George Washington. The Washington joined about 20 other ships in the Middle East, including USS George H. W. Bush, another carrier that has been there since April. Now the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group is preparing to leave its San Diego base to relieve the Washington, which is expected to finish its deployment by the end of the year. In short, the Navy is planning to maintain two aircraft carrier strike groups in the Middle East near Iran for at least the rest of 2026, U.S. officials told us. The Navy has seldom mustered such a formidable presence there since the heights of the Afghan and Iraq Wars, and the move reflects the fact that the administration is considering a ramp-up of its military-strike campaign after November, the officials said.
